audits.question: Check the entry's use of later Kiche Popol Vuh as a controlled comparison for Classic Maya myth and language; locate the manuscript/translation/era mediation rather than treating it as a Classic inscription.
audits.entry_locator: maya-classic.md §7 'Popol Vuh: creation, speech, and maize, with a chronological firewall', first bullet — "PV dates its lost alphabetic antecedent probably to 1554–1558 and Ximénez's copying/translation to 1701–1704; neither date makes the surviving manuscript Classic"; also sources bullet [PV] and §1 horizon bullet "The Popol Vuh's surviving textual history belongs here, not in a Classic archive".
audits.entry_claim: The bounded entry assertion under audit: the extant Popol Vuh is K'iche' highland literature with a colonial textual history — a lost alphabetic antecedent dated probably 1554–1558, copied and translated by Ximénez 1701–1704 — so it serves as a controlled later comparison for Classic Maya myth and language and is never treated as a Classic inscription.
audits.source_citation: Allen J. Christenson (2007), Popol Vuh: Sacred Book of the Quiché Maya People, Mesoweb electronic version (of Popol Vuh: The Sacred Book of the Maya, University of Oklahoma Press, 2003), Introduction, section 'History of the Popol Vuh Manuscript'.
audits.source_locator: Electronic edition PDF p. 27, Introduction section 'History of the Popol Vuh Manuscript'; companion 1701–1704 and transcription sentences on PDF p. 29 of the same file.
audits.source_excerpt: Although the Popol Vuh is undated, internal evidence points to the work being completed between the years 1554 and 1558.
audits.retrieval_method: Downloaded the complete 285-page electronic-edition PDF from Mesoweb with curl into the worker's ignored scratch subtree (reports/supplement-opencode-1/scratch/round6-11/), extracted full text with pdftotext -layout, located the passages by string search over per-page splits (PDF pages 27 and 29). Language: English, as rendered in the 2007 electronic edition; mediator: Mesoweb hosting of Christenson's translation/edition.
audits.basis: Christenson's own editorial dating matches both entry ranges: p. 27 gives the 1554–1558 completion range from internal evidence (cross-referenced to the Título Totonicapán signature page dated 28 September 1554 and don Juan de Rojas's disappearance from records by 1558), and p. 29 states 'Between 1701 and 1704, a Dominican monk named Francisco Ximénez, the parish priest of Chichicastenango, came to obtain the manuscript' and that he 'transcribed the Quiché text of the Popol Vuh, and added a Spanish translation'. The source therefore presents the work exactly as the entry frames it: mid-colonial K'iche' alphabetic literature surviving through an early-18th-century transcription/translation, i.e. a controlled later comparison, not a Classic inscription. The translation headings themselves are postclassic-to-colonial-horizon material, consistent with the entry's §1/§2 firewall.
audits.coupling_implication: For design use the Popol Vuh can contribute comparison motifs (maize flesh, voice-centred creation, Xibalba trials, theophoric naming) only across an explicitly declared roughly 1000-year, highland-versus-lowland gap; any Classic-period claim still needs Classic inscriptions or imagery, so fictional canon must keep the K'iche' textual horizon and the Classic court horizon as separate evidence layers rather than backdating K'iche' terms into a Classic speaker's mouth.
audits.limits: Support covers the dating and mediation claims only, not the truth of the myth itself. The lost alphabetic antecedent is inferred from internal evidence — Christenson calls the work undated — and the ranges are scholarly reconstructions, not scribal colophons. Only Christenson's introduction was inspected in this pass; no page of the Quiché transcript or of Ximénez's Ayer-volume manuscript was checked, so deeper transcription-history details (Scherzer/Brasseur chain of custody) remain outside this audit. The entry's separate Lintel 24 claims (c. 725 carving date, 28–29 October hedge) belong to other sources audited under R6-11-B corroboration, not here.

corroboration.note: Same electronic edition, companion sentence pinning the Ximénez copying/translation window
corroboration.source_excerpt: Between 1701 and 1704, a Dominican monk named Francisco Ximénez, the parish priest of Chichicastenango, came to obtain the manuscript.

questions_for_parent: Entry §10 states the Lintel 24 carving date as c. 725 CE attributed to 'the records consulted'; the Mesoweb record I inspected (see R6-11-B corroboration) does not state it. Should a later wave add a Tate 1992 / CMHI check for that specific sub-claim, or is the entry's plural-records hedge acceptable as recorded?

audits.question: Check one named jade regalia/divine-embodiment or royal costume claim using a dated object, inscription or scholarly passage; separate object provenance and visible form from an exact ancient semantic or wearer identification.
audits.entry_locator: maya-classic.md §8 'Symbolic system' table row 'Jade ↔ maize, centrality, rulership, breath | T's stated iconographic interpretation'; §9 rows 'Jade earflares/earspools' ('T relates floral flares to breath and supernatural passage') and 'Funerary jade' ('T explicitly includes funerary use and breath-spirit interpretation'); sources bullet [T] scoping the associations as 'attributed interpretations from that abstract'.
audits.entry_claim: The bounded entry assertion under audit: Taube's jade study attributes to jade the meanings maize, centrality and rulership plus a material embodiment of wind and the vitalizing breath soul; holds that floral-form jade earspools were considered supernatural sources or passageways for the breath spirit; and includes funerary use — all recorded by the entry as attributed scholarly interpretation, not as a recovered exact ancient semantic and not as a wearer identification.
audits.source_citation: Karl A. Taube (2005), 'The Symbolism of Jade in Classic Maya Religion', Ancient Mesoamerica 16(1):23–50, published abstract (DOI 10.1017/S0956536105050017).
audits.source_locator: Crossref deposit, 'abstract' field (JATS paragraph) for DOI 10.1017/S0956536105050017, sentences 3–5; the canonical article landing page https://doi.org/10.1017/S0956536105050017 refused automated fetch with HTTP 429 during this pass.
audits.source_excerpt: the Classic Maya ascribed a number of meanings to jade, including maize, centrality, and rulership, as well as a material embodiment of wind and the vitalizing breath soul
audits.retrieval_method: Cambridge Core (via doi.org) returned HTTP 429 on repeated attempts and Semantic Scholar served identity metadata only (abstract elided by publisher); the full publisher-deposited abstract text was then retrieved with curl from the public Crossref REST API endpoint, saved in the ignored scratch subtree, JATS markup stripped for reading. Language: English; text: the published abstract as deposited by the publisher; mediator: Crossref.
audits.basis: The abstract asserts every association the entry records, in the entry's own interpretive register: maize, centrality and rulership meanings plus 'a material embodiment of wind and the vitalizing breath soul'; 'Carved in floral form, jade earspools were considered supernatural sources or passageways for the breath spirit, frequently portrayed as a bead or a serpent emerging from the center of the jade flare'; and 'Because of its close relationship to the breath spirit, jade was an important component of funerary rites and the ritual conjuring of gods and ancestors'. The abstract's own verb choice ('were considered') keeps these as ancient attributed meanings inside a modern scholarly interpretation, matching the entry's 'attributed interpretations from that abstract' scoping.
audits.coupling_implication: Jade can couple to breath/maize/rulership as a multi-valent ritual-relation layer in design work, but the coupling stays interpretive and contextual: no statutory 'only kings wear jade' rule, no single fixed meaning per ornament, and funerary placement cannot be read backward as daily dress.
audits.limits: Support is abstract-scoped — exactly the entry's declared scope for [T]; the full article (pp. 23–50) was not read, so its object-by-object arguments remain unverified here. The wording was checked against the Crossref publisher deposit because the publisher page refused automated access (HTTP 429); one mediator, no independent Cambridge-side confirmation of the rendered text. The abstract asserts scholarly reconstruction of ancient intent, not proof of ancient semantics, and names no specific excavated object or wearer. Separately, per the question's demanded separation: the Mesoweb Lintel 24 record (corroboration below) supplies the dated royal-costume object side — provenance (found chipped before the east doorway of Structure 23; exhibited in the British Museum; dimensions after Graham and von Euw 1977), visible form (huipil, feather headdress, spiked rope through the tongue, blood scrolls, cache vessel with paper), and captioned ancient semantic ('the image in penance' of Itzamnaaj(?)/Kokaaj(?) Bahlam III, whose name itself carries the record's uncertainty brackets) — while it names no jade regalia and no universal wearer rule, and it does not state the entry's c. 725 carving date.

corroboration.note: Dated royal-costume object/inscription performing the question's provenance-and-visible-form versus ancient-semantic-or-wearer separation; independently retrieved passage
corroboration.source_citation: Ángel A. Sánchez Gamboa & Guido Krempel, 'Monuments of Yaxchilan: Lintel 24', Mesoweb Resources (citing Graham & von Euw 1977 and Zender 2007).
corroboration.source_locator: p. 1, 'Context:', 'Dimensions:' and description paragraphs; glyph blocks A1–H4 with transliteration and translation ('ubaah ti ch'ahbil', 'The carving of Mo' Chahk of ...l went up.')
corroboration.source_excerpt: She draws a rope through her tongue to which are fastened sharp spikes ... This blood-letting rite occurred on 5 Eb 15 Mak (9.13.17.15.12, 29 October ad 709).
corroboration.retrieval_method: Downloaded the two-page monument record PDF from Mesoweb with curl into the ignored scratch subtree and extracted text with pdftotext -layout; English/Spanish-author English rendering with Maya transliteration; mediator: Mesoweb-hosted INAH/Bonn authors' record.
corroboration.limits: Record describes pictured equipment and provenance only; it names no jade regalia, no wearer-rule, and gives no carving date (the entry's c. 725 CE remains from other records it cites). The caption date as printed here is '29 October ad 709'; the entry's '28–29 October across the records consulted' hedge is consistent but not settled by this single record.

If you want the c. 725 CE Lintel 24 carving-date sub-claim independently checked (Tate 1992 or CMHI), that is a named follow-up candidate for a later wave; this pass leaves it resting on the entry's plural-records hedge.
